title: Ideas this implies for the app
introHtml:
These are candidate features drawn from the sections above. Tick the ones worth building; we'll shape the app from what's ticked.

Decided: the app will be multilingual, with at least English, Greek, Russian and French, and a language switcher.

Decided: the interface must always be decluttered, minimal and whimsical, never crowded or packed. In practice that means one main action per screen, lots of white space, and extra options hidden until you ask for them. The whimsy comes from playful illustrations, gentle animation and friendly wording, never from extra things on screen.

Learn:

  • Guide cards covering each section of this document, short enough to read in a minute
  • Method library with what, how, evidence, best for, and an ADHD-friendly tip for each technique
  • Myth-buster cards
  • Time-cost badge on each technique (minutes per paragraph and the multiple of one recall question)
  • Further reading box on each technique with the article and paper links from this document

Explore:

  • Method Lab: start a 1 to 2 week experiment with one method
  • Session ratings (recall, enjoyment, focus, effort) and a comparison of methods
  • Keep / tweak / drop decisions and a personal "my method" profile per course or content type

Do:

  • Focus timer with a "just 5 minutes" start and a distraction parking lot
  • Blank-page recall prompt at the end of each session
  • Courses with a source map (spine, reference, videos, question bank, deck)
  • Topic list per course from learning objectives or lecture titles
  • Spaced review planner (1, 3, 7, 14, 30 days) with a "due today" list
  • Lecture lifecycle checklist (pre-read, attend, same-day recall, cards, reviews)
  • Daily top 3 and weekly plan
  • Error log for practice questions
  • Question-bank score tracker per topic
  • Exam countdown and exam-season mode

Sustain:

  • Forgiving streak (for example 5 of 7 days)
  • Done list and wins log
  • Weekly reflection (3 questions)
  • Worry dump and breathing exercise before study or exams
  • "My why" note shown on hard days
  • Points or small game elements

Technique workspaces (a small toolshed that opens for each technique you choose):

  • Active recall: a question deck you write yourself, a closed-book quiz mode, self-grading and a confidence rating per answer
  • Spaced repetition: a review queue on the 1, 3, 7, 14, 30-day rhythm with a "due today" count
  • Blank-page recall: a timed blank canvas (text and sketch), then reveal the source and mark gaps in a second colour; gap count tracked over time
  • Practice questions: a question log, an error log with cause tags (didn't know, misread, confused, ran out of time) and scores per topic
  • Interleaving: a mixer that shuffles questions from the topics you pick
  • Elaborative interrogation: a "why chain" prompt (why is this true? why? what happens if it fails?)
  • Self-explanation: step-by-step fields beside a worked example or figure
  • Feynman: a plain-words editor that flags jargon you haven't explained and keeps a list of gaps
  • Learning by teaching: a mini lesson planner, a buddy teach-back session and a short feedback form
  • Dual coding: a sketch pad beside your notes and a redraw-from-memory mode
  • Concrete examples: an example collector that asks for at least two examples from different contexts per idea
  • Pretesting: a few questions before a chapter, with a before-and-after score comparison
  • Successive relearning: a recall-until-correct loop that brings each item back on later days
  • Note templates: Cornell, question-based notes, concept map, comparison table and one-page summary
  • Memory tools: an acronym and mnemonic helper, a memory-palace builder (rooms and items) and a chunking board

Planning and focus tools:

  • Pomodoro timer with presets (25/5, 50/10, 15/5), a calm visible countdown and an optional ticking sound
  • Schedule maker: a term map from exam dates, weekly time blocks, a daily top 3, and reviews placed automatically before new material
  • Distraction parking lot available from any screen

Motivation and inspiration:

  • A short insight of the day from learning science, or an inspiring quote
  • A visual that grows with your study, for example a garden or a little creature, instead of plain charts
  • Small celebrations when a block, a review or an experiment is finished
  • A "my why" card and a wins log for hard days

Buddies (studying with other people):

  • Add buddies and see each other's study status if you choose to share it
  • Shared focus rooms: a synced Pomodoro with buddies (body doubling)
  • Co-motivation: nudges, cheers and "I'm starting now" pings
  • Co-operation: shared question decks, quizzing each other, teach-back sessions
  • Competition: friendly challenges, for example a weekly recall-score race, with an opt-in leaderboard
  • Co-competition (team play): buddies pool minutes or reviews towards a shared goal and win together
  • Privacy controls: choose what each buddy can see

AI tutors inside the tools (decided: tools that benefit from it use LLM agents):

  • Feynman coach: reads your plain-words explanation, flags jargon and gaps, and asks the follow-up a curious 12-year-old would ask
  • Socratic tutor: answers your questions with guiding questions instead of giving the answer straight away
  • Explain to a friend (teach-back): the AI plays a curious friend who interrupts with naive questions, then gives you feedback on what was unclear
  • Answer checker: grades your free-text answer against a model answer and rubric, and says what was missing
  • Question maker: turns your notes or a source into recall and pretest questions
  • Why-chain partner for elaborative interrogation, and an example coach that critiques your concrete examples
  • Examiner mode: an oral-exam or interview simulation in the subject's style
  • Error-log analyst: groups your mistakes by cause and suggests what to review
  • Method Lab coach: reads your experiment ratings and suggests the next experiment
  • Ground rules for every AI tool: you try first and the AI helps after; in recall tools it never just gives the answer; every AI tool has a simple self-check fallback when offline

Working with noema-lite (decided: this app must be compatible with noema-lite, interoperate with it and reference its features):

noema-lite is the subject engine. It holds subject packs: chapters, sections, theory blocks, 19 exercise types (7 on pictures), flashcards, debug playbooks, pitfalls, a Socratic tutor with a per-subject persona, spaced repetition keyed by section and exercise ids, sources that open at the cited page, curricula (maps of steps, each step a subject), and the learner's "About me" profile. The split is that noema-lite holds what to learn, and this app holds how to learn it, how to plan it and how to keep going.

  • Import a noema-lite subject as a course: its chapters and sections become the topic list
  • Workspaces draw on the pack: recall and pretest use its exercises and flashcards; blank-page recall uses section titles as prompts and the section text as the answer key; interleaving mixes exercises across chapters; Feynman and teach-back start from a section's mantra and objectives; scenarios come from its debug playbooks; pitfalls seed the error log
  • One shared spaced-repetition queue keyed by noema-lite ids, so nothing is scheduled twice
  • Results flow back to noema-lite: recall ratings, errors and sessions per section and exercise
  • AI tools reuse the pack's tutor settings (name, avatar, domain, what the learner already knows, examples, language) and the learner's profile
  • Source links open the original file at the cited page
  • Curricula become a course map in the schedule maker
  • Same look and feel: ADHD-friendly, minimal, one idea per screen

How the two apps connect, based on the noema-lite code (proposed):

  • Same accounts: sign in once with the noema-lite cloud account; this app keeps its own data in the same synced store under its own keys, and never overwrites noema-lite's progress records
  • Open noema-lite at the right place: a workspace button jumps straight to a section, a chapter's practice, the flashcards or the mistakes list in noema-lite
  • Read noema-lite progress (sections read, exercise results, card schedules) to suggest what to work on next
  • AI conversations saved in noema-lite's conversation format, so a Feynman session or teach-back from this app also shows up in noema-lite's history
  • Same look: noema-lite's colours, rounded cards, fonts and dark mode
  • Small changes noema-lite would need: a link to a single exercise, fixed ids for flashcards (today a card's id depends on its position), a safe way for this app to add results, and translated menus (noema-lite's buttons are English only; its AI already answers in 20 languages)

Which AI does what (decided: the app uses both Claude and Gemini, for different tasks; the split below is a proposed default):

  • Gemini for quick, structured jobs: the answer checker (the same scoring format noema-lite uses), the question maker, hints, the lightning quiz and the error-log grouping; it is fast and cheap, and noema-lite already uses it for the tutor and grading
  • Claude for long conversations and careful judgement: the Feynman coach, explain to a friend, the why-chain partner, the example coach, the examiner, the Method Lab coach and the schedule maker's term plan; and, as in noema-lite, building new subjects
  • Socratic tutor: Claude inside this app's workspaces, with a button to continue in noema-lite's own tutor (Gemini) on the same section
  • If only one key is set, every AI tool still works on that one; with no key or offline, the self-check fallback
  • Keys stay on your own device, as in noema-lite; no server holds them
